sources.title: Nigerian Senate Committee on Constitution Review, Constitution History
sources.note: 1914 amalgamation, 1922 tiny property-limited franchise, independence 1 October 1960 and republican constitution 1 October 1963.

sources.title: National Assembly Library, Nigeria’s Journey to Independence
sources.note: British conquest and January 1914 amalgamation; colonial administration through independence in 1960.

sources.title: Nigerian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, History of Nigeria
sources.note: Many earlier kingdoms, states and communities predated the 1914 colonial state.

sources.title: National Library of Nigeria, Nigeria Year Book 1963
sources.note: Contemporary Nigerian yearbook details regional constitutions, 1960 independence and 1963 republic.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Palm Oil and Protest: Women Riot 1929
sources.note: Original historical research on Ngwa women’s palm production, household spending, tax fears and the 1929 Women’s War.

sources.title: Cambridge History in Africa, The Lost Province
sources.note: Original research notes Igbo term Ogu Umunwanyi, Women’s War, for 1929 protest; modern scholarly usage.

sources.title: UNESCO, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti and the Women’s Union of Abeokuta
sources.note: Abeokuta Women’s Union mobilized tens of thousands for women’s rights and anticolonial politics.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Women, Rice, and War in Abeokuta
sources.note: Original research traces wartime food controls, women’s trade and 1947 Abeokuta tax revolt.

sources.title: University of Ibadan, Akede Eko Newspaper Collection
sources.note: Primary Yoruba newspaper issues include political reports, medicines, sports, reader letters, proverbs and cultural writing.

sources.title: Osaka University, Yoruba-Language Newspapers in Colonial Lagos
sources.note: Original press research identifies Akede Eko (The Lagos Herald), published 1928–53, and the 1920s Yoruba print boom.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Alaroye and Yoruba Newspaper Culture
sources.note: Original scholarship on I. B. Thomas’s 1929–30 Yoruba serial about Segilola and Akede Eko; title begins Itan Igbesi-Aiye Emi (Story of My Life).

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Olowe of Ise Palace Door
sources.note: Yoruba sculptor Olowe of Ise carved Ise palace doors around 1904–10 portraying royal and colonial visitors; named artist and patron.

sources.title: British Museum, Aso Oke Cloth from Nigeria
sources.note: 1920–30 Yoruba narrow-strip indigo cotton wrap with silk stripes and hand stitching; material evidence of textile skill and regional exchange.

sources.title: Nigerian Federal Ministry of Education, Education Sector Status Report
sources.note: Western Region began universal primary education 1955; Eastern and Lagos in 1957; opportunities and fees differed across regions; University College Ibadan 1948.

sources.title: National Library of Nigeria, Department of Marketing and Exports Annual Report 1950–51
sources.note: Colonial government marketing boards dealt with cocoa, oil-palm produce, groundnuts and cotton; exports reflected different farming regions.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Audience Responses to Colonial Health Films
sources.note: Original research on 1930s Lagos health films, mobile screenings and latrine-construction films; audiences did not simply accept colonial messages.

sources.title: NNPC Limited, History of Oil at Oloibiri
sources.note: First commercial oil discovery at Oloibiri in 1956, before independence.

sources.title: National Agency for the Control of AIDS, Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey 1990
sources.note: Official survey historical introduction: independence, 1963 republic, coups, Biafra civil war 1967–70, 1979 civilian government and 1983 military takeover.

sources.title: ICRC, From Biafra War Refugee to Humanitarian-Law Lecturer
sources.note: First-person memory of 1968–69 refuge, food and medicine aid, return home after 1970, and school uniforms.

sources.title: UNICEF, Sixty Years for Children: Biafra
sources.note: 1967–70 war, siege and hunger, UNICEF aid to children across political lines.

sources.title: Nigerian National Human Rights Commission, 1999 Constitution
sources.note: Official 1999 Constitution, original English preamble and democratic-rights framework.

sources.title: Nigerian Senate Committee, Constitution Chapter 2
sources.note: 1999 constitution states sovereignty belongs to Nigerians, identifies equality and diverse languages, and calls for education and welfare.

sources.title: Universal Basic Education Commission, National Personnel Audit Report 2022
sources.note: Official report explains 1999 restoration of civilian presidential rule, Nigeria’s many languages and basic-education programme.

sources.title: UNESCO, African Film: A Booming Industry
sources.note: Nollywood supports a large Nigerian film and distribution industry, around 2,500 films a year by 2021 estimates.

sources.title: WHO, Successful Ebola Responses in Nigeria
sources.note: 2014 Nigerian health teams, community radio, contact tracers and reused polio infrastructure contained imported Ebola outbreak; 20 October declaration.

sources.title: WHO Nigeria Annual Report 2020
sources.note: African Region certified free of wild poliovirus 2020 after Nigerian vaccination and surveillance; does not mean all polio forms are gone.

sources.title: UNEP, Environmental Assessment of Ogoniland
sources.note: 2011 independent assessment linked long oil operations to contaminated drinking water, land and mangroves in Ogoniland.

sources.title: Federal Ministry of Water Resources and UNICEF, WASHNORM 2021
sources.note: 2021 national survey found about 48 million people still practiced open defecation and large gaps in water and handwashing.

sources.title: Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council, National Language Policy
sources.note: Nigeria supports Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, English and many other languages in public life and education; policy aspirations are not uniform practice.

proposedOverrides.name: Colonial Nigeria
proposedOverrides.summary: British administrators combined northern and southern protectorates in 1914; the map’s c. 1920 to 1938 span is only imported coverage. Most people had no colonial vote, but women organized, Yoruba newspapers flourished and regional schools expanded. Nigeria became independent in 1960.

fell.text: Nigeria gained independence from Britain on 1 October 1960 and retained federal institutions; it became a republic in 1963.

identityEvidence.assessment: Imported label confirmed; border accuracy and local sovereignty unverified.

proposedOverrides.name: Nigeria
proposedOverrides.summary: Nigeria became independent in 1960 and a republic in 1963. It endured coups and the Biafran war from 1967 to 1970, then returned to civilian government in 1999. Film, languages, public-health achievements and continuing struggles over clean water and oil show a country far more varied than one border or headline.
